text.p: With apologies to that heavy hitter of literature, it seems Bruce Seldon doth profess too much.

Seldon knows it's crucial to have a lot of confidence to even make it out of his dressing room to take on 21-1 favourite Mike Tyson on Saturday, let alone actually exchange punches with the former undisputed heavyweight champion of the world.
So Seldon insists, like someone whistling past the graveyard where the hopes of 44 of Tyson's 45 opponents lie with stakes through their hearts, that he has confidence.
"I'm the heavyweight champion of the world. I have to have confidence," Seldon says again and again.
He's correct there. Having a good right hand and a durable chin couldn't hurt, either.
But failing those natural gifts, Seldon (33-3) continues chanting his mantra of confidence whenever he gets a chance -- whenever he opens his mouth, it seems.
Seldon is a handsome, personable and polite man, almost too polite it seemed on Thursday at a news conference for the scheduled 12-round fight at the MGM Grand.
The final news conferences before fights usually are tedious affairs filled with enough hype and promises to satisfy an army of politicians, as the fighters threaten each other with pending mayhem.
But not Seldon. Aside from an obligatory promise to hold on to his title, it seemed he paid homage to everyone he could think of.

He shook hands with Don King, even without checking afterward to see whether he still had his watch, and shook hands with Tyson, profusely thanking both men and the rest of the Tyson people on the dais for giving him an opportunity to earn $5 million on Saturday.
"You guys are great. I truly thank you for that," said Seldon, who won the vacant WBA title in April, 1995, by stopping Tony Tucker on cuts inflicted by a piercing left jab.
"I'm just going to go in there and fight my fight and see how it goes," said Seldon less than militantly.
"The harder I train the better my condition and the higher my confidence," said Seldon, again, as if he were lobbying his own mind.

Tyson, wearing a canary-yellow T-shirt and matching pants and looking bored by the proceedings, did not have much to say about his plans for Saturday night except to remind everyone, yet again, "I'm in the hurtin' business. That's what I do."

For the most part, Seldon's politeness toward the Tyson people made him mostly ignore even the insults shouted at him by a group of Tyson camp followers, whose catcalls and generally raucous behaviour would seem to be the antithesis of Tyson's professed adherence to his new Moslem religion's teachings of respect. But neither the former champion nor anyone in his camp attempted to tone down the coarse mob of Tyson supporters.

Seldon, wearing a tight black T-shirt that showed off his 50.8 cm biceps, offered up the sportsman's cliche that would seem better suited for a cricket match than a fight, saying Saturday's contest will give, "Mike Tyson an opportunity to test my skills and test himself," Seldon said.
And again he professed: "I'm a champion, I have to have confidence."
